objective: Treat bilious vomiting in a newborn as possible malrotation with volvulus and escalate for urgent surgery

brief.situation: 03:10 in a level III NICU. You are the nurse for Baby Okafor, a term boy, 3 days old, admitted for observation of transient tachypnea that has resolved. He has fed well until now.
handover: At 03:00 he vomited his whole feed; the aide says it 'looked green'. He is fussier than before and has not stooled since yesterday.

The neonatal nurse practitioner covers the unit and the pediatric surgeon is on call from home. Unit policy: the nurse may make an infant NPO and place an orogastric tube to gravity or low suction for vomiting while awaiting orders, and calls the provider at once for bilious emesis.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

then.log: Dark green, bile-stained emesis on the linen and in the basin. Not milk curds.
Abdomen soft but tender on the upper left, girth 1 cm up from the evening; no discoloration yet.
Capillary refill 3 seconds, fontanel flat, last void 4 hours ago.
Meconium passed day 1; transitional stools day 2; feeds 60 mL every 3 hours, all taken until 03:00.

why.question: What does Baby Okafor's green emesis mean, and what do you do?

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: Bilious (green) vomiting in a newborn means obstruction below the ampulla; malrotation with midgut volvulus must be ruled out at once because the twisted bowel loses its blood supply.
parts.modelAnswer: Green vomit in a newborn isn't reflux. It means a blockage, and malrotation with volvulus is the one that kills bowel within hours, so it's an emergency until a study rules it out.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Stops feeds, places an orogastric tube to suction, assesses abdomen and perfusion, and calls the provider at once asking for the surgeon and an urgent contrast study.
parts.modelAnswer: Make him NPO, put down an OG tube to suction, check his belly and perfusion, and call the nurse practitioner right now for the surgeon and an urgent upper GI.

necrosis.body: Green emesis in a newborn is malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise. NPO, decompress and call for the surgeon at once.

safe.headline: Decompressed and escalated
safe.body: You saw the bile yourself, stopped feeds, decompressed the stomach and called within minutes for the surgeon. That is the expert path.

scoring.modelReasoning: Bilious vomiting in a newborn is a surgical emergency until proven otherwise: malrotation with midgut volvulus can strangle the bowel within hours. Stop feeds, decompress the stomach with an orogastric tube, assess the abdomen and perfusion, and call the provider at once for the pediatric surgeon and an urgent upper GI contrast study. Never refeed or treat it as reflux.
